provenance: Questions in this file were adopted from the MIT-licensed project Onesayi/ccna-simulator at commit 6efca4f15e8ccf01fb44973b46bb26922797965a (Alistair Nhiwatiwa, 2026-10-04), originally authored against the CCNA v1.0 blueprint and re-keyed here to the v1.1 leaf objective IDs in src/data/objectives.json. The full per-question mapping, including every item dropped as out of scope and the reason, is in docs/ADOPTED.md. Each question records its origin in its `upstream` field. Distractor rationales are marked TODO and are written during Phase 2; no question ships without them.

questions.prompt: How do you remove just the entry with sequence number 30 from ACL 101?

questions.prompt: An ACL contains only "deny 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255" and is applied inbound. What happens to traffic from 10.2.2.5?

B.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

questions.prompt: Where should a standard ACL usually be applied?

A.text: As close to the destination as possible

B.text: As close to the source as possible

D.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

questions.explanation: Because it only checks the source, a standard ACL near the source would block that host from everything. Extended ACLs go near the source to drop traffic early.

questions.prompt: What does Dynamic ARP Inspection check ARP packets on untrusted ports against?

A.text: The routing table
A.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

B.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

C.text: The DHCP snooping binding table (and any ARP ACLs)

D.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

questions.explanation: DAI drops ARP messages whose IP-to-MAC pairing is not in the snooping bindings, which stops ARP poisoning.

questions.prompt: After DAI is enabled, a server with a static IP address loses connectivity while DHCP clients are fine. What should you add?

A.text: A static MAC address table entry
A.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

B.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

C.text: An ARP ACL permitting the server’s IP and MAC, applied with ip arp inspection filter

D.text: ip dhcp snooping trust on the server’s port and nothing else
D.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

questions.explanation: A static host never appears in the snooping table, so DAI has no binding for it. An ARP ACL (or trusting the port) lets it through.

questions.prompt: After enabling DHCP snooping on an access switch, clients behind it stop getting leases from an IOS DHCP server reached through a relay. What is a common cause?

A.text: DHCP snooping blocks all DISCOVER messages
A.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

B.text: The relay must be configured as an untrusted port
B.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

C.text: Snooping requires a static binding for every client
C.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

D.text: The switch inserts option 82 and the server rejects it; use no ip dhcp snooping information option

questions.explanation: By default the switch adds option 82 with a zero giaddr, which many servers drop.

questions.prompt: DHCP snooping is enabled. Which message arriving on an untrusted port is dropped?

A.text: DHCPOFFER

B.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

C.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

D.text: DHCPRELEASE from the client that holds the lease
D.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

questions.explanation: Server messages (OFFER, ACK, NAK) are only accepted on trusted ports, which stops rogue DHCP servers. Trust the uplink toward the real server.

questions.explanation: Bouncing the port clears err-disabled. errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation can do it automatically after an interval.

questions.prompt: In IPsec tunnel mode, what is protected?

A.text: Only the payload, keeping the original IP header
A.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

B.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

C.text: Nothing; tunnel mode only adds routing
C.rationale: TODO: explain why this is wrong

questions.explanation: Site-to-site VPNs use tunnel mode between gateways. Transport mode keeps the original header and protects only the payload, typically between two end hosts.
